title: Why the bridge ices first
text: The warning sign 'bridge ices before road' is not {{1}} caution. A bridge is exposed on all sides, so the ground {{2}} it can hold heat no longer helps: the deck {{3}} its warmth to the air above and below, while ordinary road keeps the earth's stored heat {{4}} it. As a result, on the first cold night of autumn the bridge {{5}} frost while the tarmac either side stays black and wet — and drivers, judging conditions by the road they have just {{6}}, meet ice at highway speed. The physics is the same one that {{7}} why cities stay warm: stored heat, released slowly. Engineers have tried heated decks, embedded sensors and warning signs with real-time temperature {{8}}, but the cheapest defence remains the driver's imagination: assume the bridge is icy when you cannot see that it is. The ground is a battery. Bridges are not plugged into it.

gaps.explanation: 'not gratuitous caution' — caution without cause; the physics makes the warning necessary; gregarious = sociable.
'the ground underlying it' — lying beneath the bridge; underlining = emphasising.
'the deck loses its warmth to the air' — gives it up; loosen = make less tight.
'stored heat underneath it' — below the road surface; overhead = above.
'the bridge wears frost' — takes on a coating of it, as in 'wear a coat'; wares = goods for sale.
'the road they have just traversed' — crossed; tot up = add figures (British).
'the same physics that governs why cities stay warm' — rules and explains it; gouge = scoop out.
'real-time temperature readings' — the measured values; a reading is what an instrument shows.
